content: Cysteine serves as a precursor to glutathione, a critical antioxidant that may help mitigate oxidative damage. When cysteine is added to parenteral nutrition (PN), it reduces the required amount of methionine in the solution, which can decrease hepatotoxicity. Additionally, cysteine acidifies the PN solution, enhancing the solubility of calcium and phosphate, which may contribute to improved bone mineralization. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of supplementing PN with cysteine, cystine, or its precursor N-acetylcysteine on neonatal growth and both shortand long-term clinical outcomes. A systematic search was conducted using databases such as MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, as well as abstracts from relevant pediatric and nutrition societies. The initial search was performed in 2005, with an updated search conducted in 2009. The review included all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized trials that investigated the effects of cysteine, cystine, or N-acetylcysteine supplementation in neonatal PN. Data collection and analysis followed the standard methods of the Cochrane Collaboration and its Neonatal Review Group. Statistical analyses included measures such as relative risk, risk difference, and weighted mean difference (WMD). Six trials met the inclusion criteria. Most of the participants in these studies were preterm neonates. Five small trials assessed the short-term effects of cysteine supplementation in cysteine-free PN, while one large multicenter RCT examined the short-term effects of N-acetylcysteine supplementation in cysteine-containing PN for extremely low birth weight infants (≤ 1000 grams). Cysteine supplementation did not significantly affect growth in one trial, nor did N-acetylcysteine supplementation in another trial. However, cysteine supplementation significantly improved nitrogen retention in four trials (WMD 31.8 mg/kg/day, 95% confidence interval +8.2 to +55.4, n = 95, including 73 preterm infants). Plasma cysteine levels were significantly increased with cysteine supplementation but not with N-acetylcysteine supplementation. N-acetylcysteine supplementation did not significantly alter the risks of death by 36 postmenstrual weeks, bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), combined outcomes of death or BPD, retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), severe ROP, necrotizing enterocolitis requiring surgery, periventricular leukomalacia, intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), or severe IVH. The authors concluded that available evidence from RCTs indicates that short-term cysteine chloride supplementation in cysteine-free PN improves nitrogen balance in preterm infants. However, there is insufficient evidence to evaluate the risks associated with cysteine supplementation, particularly the potential for metabolic acidosis, which has been reported during the first two weeks of cysteine chloride administration. Furthermore, evidence from a large RCT does not support the routine use of N-acetylcysteine supplementation in cysteine-containing PN for extremely low birth weight infants.
